analysis.summary: Flags non-shorthand object literal properties/methods where a shorter equivalent exists.
analysis.fixDescription: Replaces longhand property assignments with shorthand when key and variable name match ({x: x} → {x}), and replaces function expressions with method shorthand when the key is a simple identifier or computed expression matching a variable/function name ({m: function(){}} → {m()}, {[n]: function(){}} → {[n]()}).
hazards: Rewriting {a: a} to {a} changes behavior if 'a' is not in scope, causing ReferenceError.
Rewriting {b: function(){}} to {b()} alters the function's name property from 'b' to empty string, breaking reliance on func.name.
Rewriting [c]: function(){} to [c](){} may fail if 'c' evaluates to a non-string/symbol key (e.g., number), though unlikely due to rule constraints.
If the function expression contains 'use strict' directive, rewriting to method syntax may change strictness scope if surrounding context differs.
Comments attached to the function expression (e.g., {b: /* comment */ function(){}}) are lost in the fix as they are not preserved.
Rewriting getters/setters like {get x(){}} to shorthand is invalid syntax and never attempted by the fix, but if misapplied would break.
If the object literal is used in a context relying on property order (e.g., for...in), the fix preserves order so no hazard, but reordering elsewhere could.
In sloppy mode, if the property creates an implicit global via assignment, shorthand does not change this behavior, so no hazard.
If the variable 'a' in {a: a} is declared with var and used before declaration, both forms reference the same hoisted variable, so no behavioral change.
If the function expression is a generator (*), rewriting to *x(){} preserves generator nature, so no hazard.
If the key is an escaped identifier (e.g., {\u0061: a}), the fix may produce invalid syntax if not handled correctly, though ESLint avoids this.
If the object literal is nested within a with statement, property resolution changes could theoretically occur, but this is extremely rare and not specific to the fix.

results.title: this binding: arrow vs function
results.hazard: Rewriting function shorthand changes `this` binding; extracting method as const loses original `this` context.

results.title: strict vs sloppy mode semantics
results.hazard: In strict mode, `this` in function shorthand is undefined when called standalone; in sloppy mode it coerces to global, changing outcome after extraction.

results.title: implicit global in sloppy mode
results.hazard: Assignment to undeclared variable creates global in sloppy mode; shorthand rewrite doesn’t affect this since RHS reference unchanged.

findings.detail: model expected the rule to stay silent, it fired

results.title: property order reliance
results.hazard: for...in iteration order matters; rule preserves definition order, but if manually reordered post-fix, behavior diverges.

results.title: computed key with non-string/symbol
results.hazard: [c]: function(){} rewritten to [c]{} fails if c evaluates to number (coerced to string key), though rule avoids non-simple keys.

findings.detail: model expected the rule to stay silent, it fired

results.title: generator function preservation
results.hazard: Generator function shorthand rewrite {g: function*(){}} → {g*()} preserves generator nature; next() yields correctly.

results.title: getter/setter invalid shorthand
results.hazard: Rule never attempts to rewrite getters/setters; misapplication would break syntax, but here we show they remain intact.

results.title: null/undefined distinction
results.hazard: Optional chaining on rewritten shorthand method preserves nullish short-circuit behavior identically to longhand.

results.title: ReferenceError due to out-of-scope variable
results.hazard: Rewriting {a: a} to {a} changes behavior if 'a' is not in scope, causing ReferenceError.
